title: Concurrency-limited async mapping (pool pattern)
hook: Promise.all on ten thousand URLs opens ten thousand sockets and melts your API. The pool pattern caps concurrent in-flight work — a senior Node.js and LeetCode pattern that pairs with Redis pipelines, fetch batches, and backpressure.

blocks.text: **Concurrency-limited async map** processes an array of items with at most **N** asynchronous operations in flight at once. Unlike **Promise.all** which starts everything immediately, a **pool** (or **semaphore**) queues work until a slot frees. Implementations use a worker loop, a counter, or a queue of pending tasks. This is not multi-threading — still one JS thread — but limits open HTTP connections, Redis commands, and file descriptors.

entries.plainDefinition: Fixed number of concurrent async workers pulling from a shared queue.
Slowing producers when consumers are overwhelmed — pool size enforces backpressure.
entries.example: Queue depth grows if pool too small; errors spike if pool too large.

entries.plainDefinition: Counter limiting concurrent acquisitions — acquire before work, release after.
Async operations started but not yet settled.
entries.example: At most 10 fetch promises active simultaneously.

blocks.text: Bulk reindex jobs, CSV import with per-row API calls, and image thumbnail generation all need bounded concurrency. Unbounded Promise.all causes EMFILE (too many open files), Redis connection timeouts, and API rate-limit 429 storms. C# uses **SemaphoreSlim** with async WaitAsync — same idea, different primitive. Node 18+ has `p-limit` on npm; interviews want you to implement from scratch.

blocks.title: Pool size tuning
blocks.body: Start with CPU-bound vs I/O-bound: I/O pools often 5–50 depending on upstream limits. Profile p99 latency and error rate — not a universal constant.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Create pool of N workers
items.body: Each worker is an async loop pulling next index from shared cursor.

items.title: Worker acquires item
items.body: Atomically increment index or shift queue — in single-thread JS, no race.

items.title: await async work
items.body: fetch, redis.get, etc. — slot occupied until settle.

items.title: Store result, repeat
items.body: When all items processed, return results array.

snippet.label: mapPool — concurrency-limited async map
snippet.explanation: Line 7: nextIndex++ assigns unique item per worker — single-thread safe. Line 14: N worker loops run concurrently — at most N awaits in flight. Line 15: Promise.all waits for all workers to exhaust queue.

snippet.label: Production — bounded fetch with AbortSignal
snippet.explanation: Line 1: shared signal cancels all in-flight on shutdown. Line 4: pool of 10 — 10k users processed in waves, not one socket storm.

snippet.label: Semaphore variant — acquire/release
snippet.explanation: Line 6: resolve returns release function. Line 8: waiters queued when at capacity — same backpressure semantics as pool.

snippet.label: Failure mode — unbounded Promise.all
snippet.explanation: Line 2: every fetch starts at once — OS and upstream limits break. Replace with mapPool(urls, 20, url => fetch(url)).

blocks.title: Confusing pool with Worker threads
blocks.body: Pool limits concurrent async I/O on one thread. CPU-bound work needs worker_threads or breaking into chunks — pool does not use multiple cores.

blocks.title: No error strategy
blocks.body: One rejected fn fails Promise.all(workers) — decide fail-fast vs collect errors like allSettled per item.

blocks.text: Follow-ups: preserve result order (index assignment), handle early abort via AbortSignal, or dynamic pool size based on 429 Retry-After. In streaming pipelines, use async generators with manual buffer cap. Compare to Node readable stream highWaterMark. C# Parallel.ForEachAsync has MaxDegreeOfParallelism — cite it when interviewer knows .NET.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Only knowing Promise.all. Saying pool uses multiple JS threads. Cannot implement worker loop. No mention of rate limits or file descriptor limits.

interviewTakeaways: Promise.all is unbounded — pool caps in-flight async work on one thread.
Worker loop + shared index or semaphore acquire/release.
Production: pair with AbortSignal, Redis batch keys, fetch rate limits.
60s: mapPool with N workers pulling from queue. Not multithreaded — limits sockets. C# SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync same idea. Never Promise.all 10k URLs.
Follow-up: preserve order, handle per-item errors, or implement semaphore.
commonPitfalls: Weak: Promise.all for bulk — unbounded concurrency.
Weak: pool for CPU-heavy work — need Workers.
Strong: 'N async workers, shared index, await per item. AbortSignal on shutdown. Match pool to upstream limits.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: async function mapPool<T, R>(items: T[], concurrency: number, fn: (item: T, i: number) => Promise<R>): Promise<R[]>
Pool uses Promise.all on worker array — not on every item — combining both patterns.
